frau*!0From Frau by making the first letter lower-case. Coined as an alternative to the male-sounding word man,which is cognate and homophonous with Mann. First used by feminists when writing about women,then occasionally used in general contexts. Compare the pronoun mensch. Compare also the use of ''she'' vs ''he'' in English to refer to someone whose gender is unknown.é0/fraʊ̯/}Frau}Ⓓb/b3/De-Frau.ogg}Rhymes:aʊ̯|Pronoun}#indefinite one,they qualifier:indefinite third-person singular pronoun}#}@^ Sie ist selbst dann noch beschissen,wenn '''@^''' sie beendet hat.}#}• Wenn '''@^''' sich kennt  braucht sie nicht vor sich wegzulaufen.}#}• … ich ziehe es heraus und halte es in die Höhe … Mein Gott  es ist ein Still-BH. Meine Augen kleben förmlich daran. Ein Büstenhalter  den '''@^''' vorne aufmachen kann …  it is a nursing bra. My eyes were like they cleft to it. A brassière the woman can open in the front …}#}@^ Erst mal sechs Jahre alleine und '''@^''' muss auch zusehen,dass sie sich gerne hat. Das liebe ich,mit mir selbst zu sein und mich zu mögen und mich zu streicheln.}#}• … und wenn man/@^ älter wird?|Usage notes}The word is more frequently used by left-wing and/or feminist writers and speakers,which may use this word in a serious formal context,where this word is not usually acceptable,in order to express their political views. In informal context,such as magazine articles,''@^'' is usually used just once in a text as a stylistic flourish to underline that a women-specific topic is discussed.

Freunde in der Not gehen hundert auf ein Lot*{2Freunde in der Not gehen tausend auf ein Lot|Etymology}Literally:[friends in need are a hundred in a lot],meaning that a friend in need weighs 1% of a Lot (English “lot,(English)”),which is a historic measure of weight equivalent to half an ounce. One could thus loosely translate:“Friends in need are weighed in milligrams.,(English)” There are two possible interpretations:Either (a) that one’s friends become “lightweight”,i.e. unreliable,when one is in need,or (b) that true friends in need are so rare that they need to be weighed in infinitesimal quantities.é0/ˈfʁɔʏ̯ndə ˌɪn dɛɐ̯ ˈnoːt ˌɡeːən ˈhʊndɐt ˌaʊ̯f aɪ̯n ˈloːt/|Proverb}#a friend in need is a friend indeed}•synononym:in der Not erkennt man seine Freunde}rhyming phrases

Friede, Freude, Eierkuchen*German{}2014|Etymology}Literally:[peace,joy,pancakes]. The origin of the phrase is uncertain; it is attested in print at least since 1959,when the critic w:langde wrote,“Am Schluß,wie sichs gehört,Friede,Freude,Eierkuchen und Beifall” (‘At the end,as is proper,peace,joy,pancakes,and applause’).é0ˈfʁiːdə ˈfʁɔʏ̯də ˈʔaɪ̯ɐˌkuːxən+-xŋ̩}Frie+de,Freu+de,Ei+er+ku+chen|Phrase}#A-okay qualifier:often with an implication that problems are being ignored or glossed over}#}• Wir mussten nicht auf '''Friede-Freude-Eierkuchen''' machen! (We didn’t have to pretend everything was A-okay!)}#}• Und schon geht Günter wieder zur Tagesordnung über – schließlich läuft die Firma jetzt. Alles ist '''Friede  Freude  Eierkuchen'''. Der Erfolg kommt scheinbar wie von selbst  schön regelmäßig und jedes Jahr zur gleichen Saison. (And Günter is already settling into the daily routine—after all)  the company is up and running now. Everything’s A-okay. Success seems to be coming on its own  at regular intervals and at the same time every year.}#}• Familienleben bedeutet natürlich nicht nur '''Friede  Freude  Eierkuchen'''. friemeln*{2less common; unetymological|Etymology}20th century,from Low German - and from Central Franconian - dialects. Cognate to from Dutch tto fiddle,fidget. Probably the same as Dutch and posintransitive and transitive,from Low German tto rub,with a development from ''wr-'' to ''fr-'',which is widespread among dialects of all the relevant languages. Philippa (Etymologisch Woordenboek,2003-09) casts doubt on this because from Dutch wriemelen also means “to swarm” (of a collective). This collective sense need not be the oldest,however. In fact,the first attestation has the sense “to move back and forth with exertion” (of a man during sexual intercourse),and the sense “to fiddle,fidget” is attested for the ''wr''-form as well. Philippa prefers to derive from Dutch @-1en from Dutch tto fidget and this in turn from Dutch fommelen (from German fummeln). However,from Dutch frommelen shows variants with ''wr-'' as well and is also regionally more restricted.é0/ˈfriːməln/+ˈfʁiːml̩n}Ⓓe/ea/De-@^.ogg|Verb}#to fiddle; to move something in one's hands,especially by rubbing it between thumb and forefinger}•Er '''@-1te''' nervös an seinem Ohrläppchen.}•}•Sie '''@-1t''' immer mit den herumliegenden Stoffresten.}•}#by extension to do delicate manual tasks,such as inserting a thread through the eye of a needle or undoing a tangle,implying either laboriousness of the task or clumsiness of them who do it}•Ich musste ganz schön '''@^''',um das auseinanderzukriegen.}•|Derived terms}auseinander@^}Friemelei}herum@^}rein@^

fudeln*{2rarer spelling,but common pronunciation; see below|Etymology}From Low German to work negligently and from Central Franconian to work negligently; to cheat; to use contraception. The verb may be derived from Low German Fudde,from Central Franconian Fudd,from Central Franconian Fuddel,all “rag,old cloth” (compare from Dutch vod); plausibly through a sense “to brush superficially with a rag”,as there existed a particular association with houseworkers. However,the verb reaches much further south along the Rhine than does the noun and many forms require an underlying long vowel. Many dialects also have several forms alongside. Therefore the above seems to have been influenced by or merged with one or more other verbs,including perhaps one from Old French tfault,misbehaviour. Compare from Luxembourgish fuddelen,from Luxembourgish fautelen,from Luxembourgish pautelen,all “to cheat”.é0/ˈfuːdl̩n/+/ˈfʊdl̩n/}Rhymes:uːdl̩n|Verb}#to cheat,usually at a game}•synononym:[mogeln],[betrügen]}#possibly to work negligently|Derived terms}Fudelei}Fudler

garen*!0From gar,`b prepared. Not related to gären.é0Ⓓ1/17/De-@^.ogg|Verb}#transitive cook Literally:[prepare (food) for eating]}•synononym:kochen}•Wir haben die Kartoffeln im Backofen '''gegart'''.}•We cooked the potatoes in the oven.}#intransitive cook Literally:[become ready for eating]|Usage notes}''Garen'' and kochen both mean "to cook (food)",but the emphasis is different. ''Kochen'' is very general,covering all aspects of cooking and focusing on the entire process of preparing food to be eaten. ''Garen'' emphasizes the thorough heating of food; food that is ''gegart'' is "done" in the sense of completely cooked. Because ''kochen'' can also mean "boil",''@^'' must be used when referring to a heating process other than boiling. ''Wir haben die Kartoffeln im Backofen '''gekocht''''' would not make sense,since one boils potatoes on the stove top and not in the oven.

Gehalt*@0ɡəˈhalt}Ⓓa/a2/De-@^.ogg|Etymology 1}'''@^''' m. 'content,share',late Middle High German. '''gehalt''' 'custody,prison,inner value' is a verbal abstract of Middle High German '''gehalten''' 'to keep still,to hold,to preserve,to imprison' (by prefix strengthened halten,`b '''gihalto''' 'keeper,guardian',9th cent.). Correspondingly,still today South German '''@^''' stands for 'container' (e.g. 'room,cupboard'). Today's meaning 'constituent,content' develops in the 15th c. It first applies to the silver or gold content of coins,in the 17th c. to the content of chemical substances in a mixture; in the 18th c. the figurative use common today is encountered (cf. inner content,the true content of words,content and form). To keep in the sense of 'maintain' belongs '''@^''' n. 'salary,income' (18th c.,initially also m.),actually 'maintenance without consideration',cf. gracious,widow's salary (18th c.).|Noun}n:min Austria,(e)s,^er,genitive:@^es,plural:[Gehälter])}#salary£7[@^(e)s])}#content

gehen*{2geh'n}dated in formal prose,but still common informally and poetically|Etymology}from Proto-Indo-European ⋆ǵʰengʰ-}<4gān,£9 gēn,`b gān,`b gēn,é7 ⋆gān,from Proto-Germanic ⋆gāną,from Proto-Indo-European to leave.}Cognate with from Dutch gaan,from Low German gan,from Low German gahn,from English go,Swedish and Danish from Swedish gå.}The form ''gēn'' instead of ''gān'' is of Bavarian origin,but many dialects of Central and Low German have ''-e-'' (from earlier ''-ei-'') or ''ei'' in the 2nd and 3rd person singular present,in keeping with the Proto-Germanic irregular conjugation. The ''-h-'' was introduced into the spelling by analogy with sehen,in which it had become mute but was retained in spelling.é0/ˈɡeːən/,ˈɡeː.ən,(official standard) but less common}/ɡeːn/,ɡeːn,(predominant)}Rhymes:eːəneːn}ge+hen}Ⓓ5/5f/De-@^2.ogg|Verb}@^(ging,gegangen,auxiliary:sein)}#intransitive to go,to walk}•Lass uns beide mit dem Hund '''@^'''.}•Let's '''walk''' the dog together.}•Ich sah die Kinder über die Straße '''@^'''.}•I saw the children '''walk/go''' across the street.}•Mein Baby beginnt schon zu '''@^'''.}•My baby is already starting to '''walk'''.}#intransitive to leave}•Ich '''gehe''' jetzt.}•I’m '''leaving''' now.}#intransitive to leave,to take off Literally:[aeroplane,train]}•synononym:[fahren],[abfahren]}•Wann '''geht''' dein Zug?}•When is your train '''leaving'''?}#impersonal to be going; to be all right @^ ( with  datfor someone+predicate&adjectivein a particular way) idiomatically translated by m+ or similar,with the dative object as the subject}•Wie '''geht''' es dir?}•How are you doing?}•Es '''geht''' mir gut.}•I’m doing well.}•litIt goes well for me.}•Es '''geht'''.}•It’s all right.}#slightly to be possible}•Das würde vielleicht '''@^'''.}•That might '''be possible'''.}•Ich zeige dir,wie es '''geht'''.}•I'll show you how it's '''possible'''.}#colloquial to work,to function Literally:[of a machine,method or the like]}•synononym:funktionieren}•Der Kaffeeautomat '''geht''' nicht.}•The coffee dispenser doesn't '''work'''.}#}• Aber erst in Beirut lernte sie  wie professionelles Kochen '''geht'''  die Logistik  das Timing  die Organisation  um mehrere Hundert Mahlzeiten zuzubereiten. A distinction must be made between ''@^'' (walk),fahren (go by bike,car,train,or ship),and fliegen (go by plane). Gelichter*£3 tsiblings,kin,`b twomb,matrix,a derivative of `b ligan,modern liegen. Since the seventeenth century often despective.é0/ɡəˈlɪçtɐ/}Ⓓ7/74/De-@^.ogg|Noun}(neut.)}#kind,genus}#}@^ Die grosse Schwierigkeit,welche der Ackerbau in Biscaya zu überwinden hat,ist die Härte und Strenge des Bodens. Sie durchpflügen ihn daher nicht nur mehreremale nach einander,sondern bedienen sich auch dazu einiger ganz eigener Werkzeuge. Das eigenthümlichste unter denselben ist die ''laya''. Sie besteht aus einer langen und spitzigen zweizackigen Gabel mit einem kurzen Stiel,der aber nicht in der Mitte,sondern an dem einen Ende befestigt ist. Jeder Arbeiter hat zwei solche Gabeln in der Hand,sticht sie horizontal in die Erde ein,drückt sie,mit einem,oder auch wohl mit beiden Füssen zugleich darauf tretend,noch tiefer ein,und reisst dann,den Stiel nach sich zu niederdrückend,ein ganzes grosses Rasenstück auf einmal los und wendet es herum. Diese schon durch das stete Bücken äusserst beschwerliche Arbeit wird immer,wie bei uns das Graben,zugleich von mehreren verrichtet,und daher kommt das in die Spanische Sprache übergegangene Sprichwort:lang:es:''son de una misma laya,'' sie sind eines '''@^s'''.|translationThe great difficulty which soil cultivation has to surmount in Biscaya,is the hardness and strength of the bottom. They till it therefore not only multiple times in succession,but also employ some peculiar instruments. The most peculiar under them is the ''laya''. It consists in a long and spiky two-pronged fork with a short shaft,which however isn’t fastened in the middle,but at one end. Each labourer has two such forks in his hand,sticks them horizontally into the earth,pushes them,with one,or peradventure with both feet simultaneously treading on them,even deeper,and tears then,pushing the shaft down to him,a whole bit of lawn at once aloose and turns it over. This job onerous already by way of the constanting stooping is always,as with us graving,performed at the same time by many,and hence comes the saying passed into Spanish:lang:''son de una misma laya,'' they are of one '''kind'''.}#throng,mob,vulgus,who follows

gemischte Deklination*@0/ɡəˈmɪʃtə deklinaˈtsi̯oːn/}Ⓓ9/9d/De-@_.ogg|Noun}gemischte<+> Deklination<f.article>,strong)}#mixed declension}#German a type of declension that adjectives use after ein,kein,and possessive determiners}#German a type of noun declension with -en in the plural,but -s,-es,-ens in the genitive singular}#Latin a subclass of the third declension of nouns and adjectives|Usage notes}With regard to German adjectives,the term “mixed declension” is generally used for simplicity. A closer analysis shows,however,that there are in fact just two declensions,strong and weak,but that there is a general rule prescribing that determiners with no declensional ending must be followed by strong adjectives,even if they are otherwise followed by weak ones.
